traditions.label: Albanian Greek Catholic tradition (Southern Albania / Elbasan mission)
traditions.scope: Historical Byzantine Catholic community of Southern Albania (Elbasan St. Peter mission and the 1939 Apostolic Administration of Southern Albania), strictly separate from Italo-Albanian eparchies (Lungro, Piana) and the Albanian Orthodox Church.
traditions.coverage_note: Zero documented or provisional liturgical-book stages: two dedicated prior research rounds and fresh verification confirmed institutional and archival leads (1939 Inter regiones, Scarpelli 1928–1929, Papamihali 1936–1946, DGA 2007 archive census) but authenticated no Catholic Albanian celebrant edition. Orthodox Albanian and Italo-Albanian books are deliberately excluded.

traditions.label: Macedonian Greek Catholic Church (Strumica–Skopje)
traditions.scope: Official Holy See approval/recognitio of Macedonian Divine Liturgies (9 December 2009) and unresolved pre-2009 Slavonic and post-2009 printed Macedonian service-book identity.
traditions.coverage_note: One documented approval-act stage (9 December 2009) verified in SICO 2009 and the official Congregation register. The reported 2009 printed Liturgikon title, its Greek or Church Slavonic exemplar, pre-2009 Strumica/Križevci Church Slavonic usage, and dated operative altar use remain open gaps.

traditions.label: Belarusian lands: Kyivan Uniate and modern Belarusian Greek Catholic books
traditions.scope: Church Slavonic Uniate Sluzhebniks printed in Vilnius, Supraśl, and Pochaiv (1617–1788) in the historical Kyivan Metropolitan Province, plus a provisional lead for modern Belarusian Greek Catholic liturgical translations.
traditions.coverage_note: Four documented historical printing states (1617, 1727–1732, 1758, 1788) with bounded primary-image and scholarly evidence connected to the 1692–1695 Vilnius–Supraśl and 1754 Roman Greek baselines, plus one provisional modern Belarusian lead (Nadson 2005). 1796–1839 Uniate printing and modern ecclesiastical approval remain open gaps.

traditions.label: Byzantine Catholic Church of Croatia and Serbia (Križevci Eparchy and Ruski Krstur)
traditions.scope: Reception of Roman Ruthenian Church Slavonic exemplars (1942, 1970) in officially approved Croatian (2018) and Slovenian (2022–2023) liturgical books of the Križevci Eparchy, with Serbia (Eparchy of St. Nicholas in Ruski Krstur) kept explicitly distinct.
traditions.coverage_note: Four documented stages (1965 Slovenian, 1970 Rome Ruthenian exemplar, 2018 Croatian Chrysostom, 2022–2023 Slovenian Služebnik) and four documented transitions showing reception of Rome 1942/1970 and concrete Slovenian antiphon/Proskomedia revisions. Pre-1942 Križevci Slavonic books (distinct from Parčić's 1894 Roman Glagolitic missal) and Ruski Krstur Serbian Rusyn altar books remain explicit gaps.

traditions.label: Georgian Byzantine-rite Catholic historical community (non-sui iuris)
traditions.scope: Historical Byzantine-rite Georgian Catholic diaspora and Constantinople (Feriköy) monastery press context (from 1861/1870); explicitly NOT an autonomous sui iuris Eastern Catholic Church.
traditions.coverage_note: Contextual historical note and explicit bibliographic gap only; zero book stages asserted until individual Constantinople or Montauban Byzantine-rite Georgian Catholic liturgical imprints are catalogued and inspected.

stages.label: Meletios Karmé's Arabic Liturgikon revision
stages.scope: Historical Arabic Liturgikon recension prior to the 1724 Antiochian split; shared baseline cited by Charon when analyzing 1701 and later Melkite printings.
stages.witness_label: Arabic Liturgikon revision of Meletios (Malatios) Karmé (1612), preface quoted in Charon (1908)
stages.summary: Metropolitan Meletios Karmé revised the Arabic Liturgikon against Greek sources; Charon quotes the preface and identifies Karmé's Arabic recension as the Arabic text later printed at Snagov in 1701.

evidence.claim: Quotes Karmé's preface, dates the Liturgikon revision to 1612, and identifies it as the Arabic text printed in 1701.

stages.limitations: Pre-1724 shared Antiochian manuscript recension, not a Catholic-exclusive printing. Original manuscripts and Karmé's separate 1630s–1643 Euchologion project (Vat. ar. 618) were not collated by this project.
stages.reception: Shared Antiochian Arabic heritage received into printed circulation in 1701 and used by both Orthodox and Catholic Melkites prior to 1839.

stages.label: Snagov Greek–Arabic Liturgikon of Athanasios Dabbas
stages.date_label: 1701 publication (later used in 1743 Roman correction project)
stages.scope: First printed Greek–Arabic Liturgikon containing Chrysostom, Basil, and Presanctified; Arabic follows Karmé while Greek follows a Venice edition (non-parallel columns).
stages.witness_label: The three Divine Liturgies in Greek and Arabic, Athanasios Dabbas (Snagov, 1701)
stages.summary: Printed in Wallachia under Patriarch Athanasios Dabbas combining Karmé's Arabic text with a Venice Greek edition; Charon documents its use among Melkite Catholics and describes the annotated Greek College copy prepared for the unprinted 1743 Demandatam correction project.

evidence.claim: Identifies the 1701 Snagov Greek–Arabic printing, distinguishes its Arabic (Karmé) and Greek (Venice) texts, attests Melkite Catholic usage, and describes the annotated 1743 project copy.

stages.limitations: Pre-1724 printing shared across Antioch; the 1743 bull Demandatam ordered a corrected Roman printing that did not appear in 1743. Original 1701 scan not independently collated.
stages.reception: Explicitly attested in Melkite Catholic use by Charon until superseded by Propaganda Fide's 1839 printing.

stages.label: Choueir (Shuwayr) Monastery Press Arabic lectionary and proper books (Zakher press)
stages.scope: Complementary Eucharistic lectionary and proper books printed at Dayr Mar Yuhanna al-Sabigh (Choueir/Shuwayr): Apostolos (1759), Small Octoechos (1767), Book of Prophecies (1775), Gospels (1776), and Horologion (1787). Explicitly distinct from an altar Liturgikon.
stages.witness_label: Choueir Basilian Monastery Arabic liturgical series (Apostolos 1759, Octoechos 1767, Prophecies 1775, Gospels 1776, Horologion 1787)
stages.summary: Following Abdallah Zakher's establishment of the Choueir Arabic press in 1733–1734 (first titles Mīzān al-zamān 1734 and Psalter 1735), the monastery issued the Melkite Catholic complementary reading and proper corpus—Apostolos (1759, Zakher's revision, five identical printings to 1859), Small Octoechos (1767, 1784), Book of Prophecies (1775, reproducing Dabbas 1708), Gospels (1776, 1818, 1861), and Horologion supplying apolytikia and kontakia (1787, 1852, 1879)—all without the Propaganda imprimatur mandated by Benedict XIV.

evidence.claim: Catalogues the Choueir printings of the Apostolos (1759–1859), Octoechos (1767, 1784), Prophecies (1775–1833), Gospels (1776–1861), and Horologion (1787–1879), noting Zakher's revisions and absence of Roman imprimatur.

stages.limitations: Complementary lectionary and proper books only—NOT an 18th-century Shuwayr Liturgikon (no 1733, 1745, or 1764 Choueir Liturgikon is attested in Charon; 1745 is Orthodox Patriarch Sylvester's Iaşi Hieratikon, and 1764 at Choueir is Zakher's theological work Al-Burhān al-ṣarīḥ). Original Choueir copies remain unacquired.
stages.reception: Repeated identical reprints over a century attest sustained Melkite Catholic liturgical reliance on the Choueir press for readings and propers despite lack of Propaganda imprimatur.

stages.label: Propaganda Fide Greek–Arabic Liturgikon
stages.scope: First printed Catholic-revised Greek–Arabic altar Liturgikon (280 pp.), introducing papal commemoration, removing diptychs, and conforming communion prayers to the Roman Greek Euchologion.
stages.witness_label: Greek–Arabic Liturgikon (Rome: Propaganda Fide, 1839), 280 pp.
stages.summary: Propaganda Fide published the revised Melkite Greek–Arabic Liturgikon (accompanied by a Chrysostom offprint omitting prothesis), adding papal commemoration, suppressing the diptychs, and conforming communion prayers to the Roman Greek Euchologion text.

evidence.claim: Documents the 1839 Rome Propaganda printing (280 pp.) and specifies papal commemoration, removal of diptychs, and communion-prayer conformity to the Roman Greek text.

stages.limitations: Scholarly description by Charon; original 1839 Arabic–Greek volume not independently acquired or collated by this project.
stages.reception: Provided the textual base for the 1862 Vienna reprint and the 1880 Choueir Chrysostom printing.

stages.label: Vienna Greek–Arabic Liturgikon (reprint of Propaganda 1839)
stages.scope: 288-page quarto reprinting Propaganda 1839 in identical typographic disposition for free distribution to Melkite Catholic churches.
stages.witness_label: Greek–Arabic Liturgikon (Vienna: Imperial and Royal Press, 1862), 288 pp.
stages.summary: Edited by priests Moïse Maqhat and Philippe Noumeir under Patriarch Clement Bahouth and Bishop Basil Chahiat (letter of 22 February 1862) and funded by the Archbishop of Esztergom and Hungarian bishops, deliberately reproducing the 1839 Propaganda Liturgikon text and layout (with a companion 179-page Chrysostom extract).

evidence.locus: Printed pp. 575–580, table p. 591 (citing preface pp. 2–3)
evidence.claim: Transcribes the 22 February 1862 preface data and confirms that Vienna 1862 deliberately reprints the 1839 Propaganda text and disposition.

stages.limitations: Reprint witness, not a substantive textual revision; original 1862 copy not acquired. Corrects secondary confusion labelling this 1862 Vienna book a Typikon.
stages.reception: Printed for free distribution across Melkite Catholic churches; exact parish-level distribution unquantified.

stages.label: Great Arabic Euchologion (Jerusalem: Franciscan Press)
stages.scope: Complementary priestly/sacramental Euchologion (326 pp.) explicitly excluding the Divine Liturgies (Liturgikon); based on the Roman Greek Euchologion with Melkite adaptations of chorepiscopal and other orders.
stages.witness_label: Great Arabic Euchologion (Jerusalem: Franciscan Press, 1865), 326 pp.
stages.summary: Issued at the Jerusalem Franciscan Press following the 1851 Propaganda Small Arabic Euchologion, supplying the wider Melkite priestly ritual based on the Roman Greek book with Melkite chorepiscopal adaptations while keeping the Eucharistic Liturgikon in a separate book.

evidence.claim: Distinguishes the 1865 Jerusalem Great Euchologion (326 pp.) from Karmé's Vat. ar. 618 and notes its Roman Greek basis, Melkite chorepiscopal adaptations, and explicit exclusion of Liturgikon contents.

stages.limitations: Complementary priestly ritual rather than an altar Liturgikon; original 1865 volume and Charbel Nassif's 2022 OpenEdition study (efr/46083) remain to be read in full.
stages.reception: Major 19th-century Melkite Catholic Euchologion; predecessor context for the 1968 Paulist revision.

stages.label: Mo'aqqad Arabic Menaia and revised Horologion
stages.scope: Patriarchally approved Melkite Catholic Arabic proper books (875-page anthology-type Menaia and 736-page revised Horologion) supplying Eucharistic troparia, kontakia, and Typika psalms.
stages.witness_label: Melkite Catholic Arabic Menaia (Beirut: Shaker Batlouni, 1883) and Arabic Horologion revised by Germanos Mo'aqqad (1883)
stages.summary: Approved by Patriarch Gregory II Youssef and revised by Archimandrite Ignatius (Germanos) Mo'aqqad (1881–1883): the Menaia present an anthology selection omitting synaxaria, vigil readings (kept in Book of Prophecies), and Royal Hours; the revised Horologion corrects the Arabic, restores Psalms 33 and 144 to the Typika, and inserts troparia of proper Melkite Catholic offices.

evidence.claim: Documents Gregory II Youssef's approvals and details the specific omissions in the 1883 Menaia and the restored Typika psalms and Melkite Catholic proper troparia in the 1883 Horologion.

stages.limitations: Scholarly description by Charon; original 1883 volumes and subsequent reprints (Menaia 1896, abridged Menaia 1898, Horologion 1890/1898/1905) remain unacquired.
stages.reception: Approved by Patriarch Gregory II Youssef and repeatedly reprinted into the early 20th century.

stages.label: Rahmé Arabic Liturgikon (Beirut: Jesuit Press)
stages.scope: Revised Arabic altar Liturgikon edited by Michael Ibrahim Rahmé (343 pp. in 1900; parallel 300 pp. small format in 1899), with undated permission of Patriarch Peter IV Geraigiry.
stages.witness_label: The Divine Liturgies of Michael Ibrahim Rahmé (Beirut: Jesuit Press, 1899–1900)
stages.summary: Restyles Arabic rubrics without altering sense, corrects spelling and grammar in prayers, prints the diaconal litany in full, adds a preface and appendix, and inserts at pp. 140–141 a commemoration formula for Pope, patriarch, and bishop expressly annotated as absent from Propaganda 1839. Later cited by Patriarch Gregorios III's Letter on the Liturgy as a milestone edition.

evidence.locus: Printed pp. 584–591, table p. 591 (noting pp. 140–141 commemoration formula)
evidence.claim: Details Rahmé's 1899/1900 parallel formats, patriarchal permission, restyled rubrics, full diaconal litany, and added Pope–Patriarch–Bishop commemoration formula.
Official patriarchal retrospective recognizes Rahmé's 1900 Liturgikon in the Melkite service-book lineage.

stages.limitations: Original 1899/1900 copies unacquired; Charon notes he never heard the pp. 140–141 formula actually used in liturgy, proving that print presence does not equal universal observance.
stages.reception: Issued with undated patriarchal permission of Peter IV Geraigiry and recognized retrospectively by Patriarch Gregorios III.

stages.label: Badaouy Melkite Catholic Pentecostarion (1900), Apostolos (1902), and Triodion (1903)
stages.scope: Patriarchally approved Catholic Arabic seasonal proper and epistle books edited by Khalil Badaouy, replacing Melkite Catholic reliance on Orthodox Jerusalem printings (1854, 1856) and Zakher's Choueir Apostolos (1759–1859).
stages.witness_label: Melkite Catholic Pentecostarion (1900, 314 pp.), Apostolos (1902, 302 pp.), and Triodion (1903, 611 pp.), ed. Khalil Badaouy
stages.summary: Approved by Patriarch Peter IV Geraigiry: the 1900 Pentecostarion removes synaxaria and appends the office of the Most Holy Sacrament (Corpus Christi); the 1902 Apostolos replaces Abdallah Zakher's Arabic biblical text with the Jesuit Arabic Bible and shortens Sunday prokeimena; the 1903 Triodion removes synaxaria, replaces Gregory Palamas with Maximos III Mazloum's office of the Holy Relics, and omits the Synodikon of the Sunday of Orthodoxy.

evidence.claim: Records Peter IV Geraigiry's approvals and specifies the exact structural, scriptural, and calendar changes across all three Badaouy volumes.

stages.limitations: Charon did not have the Badaouy Pentecostarion and Triodion in hand when writing; original books and signed approvals remain unacquired.
stages.reception: First Melkite Catholic printed Pentecostarion and Triodion replacing previously used Orthodox Jerusalem editions (1854, 1856).

stages.label: Harissa renewal decree (1956) and Synodal Divine Liturgy decrees (1969, 1970, 1972)
stages.scope: Normative Melkite patriarchal and synodal decrees reshaping Divine Liturgy execution prior to the 1992–2007 books: liturgical renewal principles (1956), permitted abbreviations (1969/1970), aloud presbyteral prayers and post-epiclesis prostration (1970), and communion formula rule (1972).
stages.witness_label: Decrees of Maximos IV (Harissa 1956) and Holy Synod (1969, 1970, 1972), preserved in Patriarch Gregorios III's Letter on the Liturgy
stages.summary: Patriarch Maximos IV set out renewal principles at Harissa (1956); the Holy Synod subsequently enacted standardized liturgical abbreviations from early 1970 while permitting the full old text and ordering a corrected booklet (1969), directed named presbyteral prayers to be spoken aloud with a deep prostration after the epiclesis (1970), and affirmed 'the servant of God' while forbidding 'the son of God' in the communion formula (1972).

evidence.claim: Reproduces the 1956 Harissa principles and summarizes the 1969, 1970, and 1972 synodal enactments on abbreviations, aloud prayers, post-epiclesis prostration, and communion wording.

stages.limitations: Known here through the English official retrospective of 2010/2011; original Arabic synodal decrees and the ordered 1969/1970 booklet were not acquired.
stages.reception: Patriarchal and synodal norms for the Melkite Church; the 1969 decree explicitly left the older unabbreviated text optional.

stages.label: Experimental Book of the Divine Liturgies
stages.scope: Commission-prepared experimental Arabic Liturgikon introducing variable presbyteral prayers and unified liturgical rubrics ahead of the 2001 definitive synodal text.
stages.witness_label: Experimental Book of the Divine Liturgies (1992; decree of 1991 reported in patriarchal Letter)
stages.summary: Following 1987–1988 commission studies, the Patriarchal Liturgical Commission issued an experimental Arabic Book of the Divine Liturgies incorporating variable presbyteral prayers and revised rubrics for trial use across the patriarchate prior to definitive 2001 synodal approval.

evidence.claim: Reports the 1987–1988 studies, the 1991 use decree, and the 1992 experimental text with variable prayers and liturgical directions.

stages.limitations: The patriarchal letter dates the use decree to 1991 and the experimental text to 1992; both dates are preserved without harmonization pending inspection of the original Arabic title leaf and decree.
stages.reception: Authorized for experimental patriarchal use prior to the definitive 2001 approval and 2006–2007 printed volumes.

stages.label: Unified Melkite Liturgical Prayer Books (four volumes in six parts)
stages.scope: Modern Arabic complementary proper and office corpus (Horologion, Paraklitike, Menaion, Triodion, Pentecostarion) translated/corrected from the Greek original into four volumes (six physical parts) at Jounieh.
stages.witness_label: Kitāb al-ṣalawāt al-taqdīsiyya (Jounieh: Paulist Press, 1997–2000; DLI record 44455)
stages.summary: Issued with permission of Patriarch Maximos V (1996 decree mandating exclusive use from Pascha 1997; reaffirmed in 2011) as a 'corrected translation on the basis of the Greek original language', consolidating seasonal Menaia, Octoechos/Paraklitike, Triodion, and Pentecostarion propers into six chronologically sequenced parts printed 1997–2000.

evidence.claim: Records the 1996 decree, Pascha 1997 exclusive-use mandate, and four-volume/six-part organization.
Supplies exact Jounieh Paulist Press publication years (1997, 1998, 1999, 2000), pagination, Maximos V permission, and Greek-original correction statement.

stages.limitations: Complementary office and proper corpus, not the altar Liturgikon; original Arabic volumes remain unacquired and uncollated against the 1883–1903 editions.
stages.reception: Declared exclusive for Melkite use by Patriarch Maximos V (1996) and reaffirmed by Patriarch Gregorios III (7 March 2011).

stages.label: Third Blaj Romanian Cyrillic Liturghier (under Bishop Ioan Bob)
stages.scope: Third Romanian Cyrillic Blaj printing of the Divine Liturgies, continuing the early Blaj textual line before the 1870 Latin-script revision.
stages.witness_label: Dumnezeeştile Liturghii (Blaj, 1807, third printing)
stages.summary: Printed at Blaj under Bishop Ioan Bob as the third Blaj edition; Ioan Bălan's 1915 comparison groups 1756, 1775, and 1807 together as close copies of Antim's Liturghier with minor corrections, prior to the sharp linguistic and rubrical break of 1870.

evidence.claim: Places 1807 with 1756 and 1775 as early Blaj printings closely following Antim's text with limited corrections.

evidence.locus: Printed pp. 95–104, Table 1 and Aușeu parish purchase note (1857)
evidence.claim: Lists Blaj 1807 in the Blaj Liturghier sequence and reports parish acquisition at Aușeu on SS. Peter and Paul 1857.

stages.limitations: Original 1807 scan and title leaf remain unacquired; grouped with 1756/1775 on Bălan's testimony without project-level collation.
stages.reception: Blaj Greek Catholic printing attested in Oradea-area parish circulation (Aușeu purchase 1857); wider diocesan adoption unquantified.

stages.label: Blaj Latin-script revised Liturghier with Latinizing vocabulary and added blessing
stages.scope: Substantive linguistic and ritual revision printed in Latin script with etymological orthography (Blasiu, MDCCCLXX), introducing Latinizing vocabulary and an added blessing of the people with the gifts.
stages.witness_label: Domnedieescile si sântele liturgii … Ioane Crisostomu, Basiliu celu Mare, Gregoriu Dialogulu (Blasiu, 1870)
stages.summary: Marks a substantial break from the 1756–1807 Cyrillic line: beyond shifting to etymological Latin orthography, Ioan Bălan (1915) documents deliberate Latinizing alterations to liturgical vocabulary and the insertion of a rubrical blessing of the people with the consecrated gifts; Sana (2013) documents local parish resistance to its adoption.

evidence.claim: Documents the substantive Latinizing vocabulary shift and the added blessing of the people with the gifts in Blaj 1870.

evidence.locus: Printed pp. 95–104, Table 1 and reception discussion
evidence.claim: Lists Blaj 1870 and records parish resistance to the altered wording.

stages.limitations: Original 1870 copy not acquired; textual and rubrical changes rest on Bălan's 1915 comparative study rather than independent page collation.
stages.reception: Official Blaj edition that encountered documented local reception resistance in Oradea parishes (Sana 2013).

stages.label: Blaj moderated-wording Liturghier
stages.scope: Linguistic moderation of the 1870 Blaj Liturghier, revising prayer wording away from extreme 1870 Latinisms.
stages.witness_label: Liturghier (Blaj, 1905)
stages.summary: Revises and moderates the heavily Latinized vocabulary of the 1870 Blaj edition, altering prayer wording; named by Neagu (2019) as the direct predecessor replaced by the 1931 interdiocesan Liturghier.

evidence.claim: Documents the 1905 moderation of 1870 vocabulary and concrete changes in prayer wording.
Identifies Blaj 1905 as the preceding official edition prior to 1931.

stages.limitations: Original 1905 volume unacquired; exact inventory of changed rubrics vs 1870 remains uncollated.
stages.reception: Standard Blaj Liturghier between 1905 and 1931; local adoption rates unquantified.

stages.label: Interdiocesan standardized Blaj Liturghier (Metropolitan Vasile Suciu / Stâna de Vale commission)
stages.scope: Interdiocesan rubrical and linguistic standardization across all Romanian Greek Catholic dioceses, later retained as the linguistic baseline for the 1996 and 2014 editions.
stages.witness_label: Liturghier (Blaj, 1931; Metropolitan Vasile Suciu, preface by Canon Victor Macaveiu)
stages.summary: Prepared by an interdiocesan commission meeting at Stâna de Vale representing all Romanian Greek Catholic dioceses, completing rubrics only where uniform practice existed and stabilizing Romanian liturgical language; critiques reached the Episcopal Conference of 4 November 1931. Later affirmed as approved by synodal circular 68/2009 and cited by the 2015 circular as the linguistic foundation retained in 1996 and 2014.

evidence.claim: Firsthand account of the Stâna de Vale interdiocesan commission's rubric completion and the 4 November 1931 Episcopal Conference review.

evidence.locus: Discussion of 1931 Liturghier citing Unirea 20 June 1931
evidence.claim: Confirms Blaj 1931 with Macaveiu's preface succeeding 1905.
Confirms that the 1996 and 2014 editions retain the linguistic tradition of Metropolitan Vasile Suciu's 1931 Liturghier.

stages.limitations: Original 1931 printed volume and any Roman approval instrument remain unacquired. No standalone 1937 Blaj Liturghier is evidenced (1931 is the interwar Liturghier milestone).
stages.reception: Explicitly recognized as approved in circular 68/2009 and foundational for post-1989 Romanian Greek Catholic editions.

stages.label: Rome Romanian Greek Catholic Liturghier
stages.scope: Post-1989 official Romanian Liturghier printed in Rome, retaining the 1931 linguistic tradition and named as the immediate predecessor of Blaj 2014.
stages.witness_label: Liturghier (Rome, 1996)
stages.summary: Named by the 20 May 2015 synodal circular as the previous official edition replaced by Blaj 2014, and listed alongside Blaj 1931 as an approved Liturghier by circular 68 of 21 November 2009; retains Vasile Suciu's 1931 linguistic line.

evidence.claim: Identifies Rome 1996 as the preceding edition and links its linguistic line to Blaj 1931.
Reports circular 68/2009 recognizing the 1931 and 1996 editions as approved.

stages.limitations: Original 1996 volume and front matter remain unacquired; shared 1931 linguistic continuity does not establish byte-level textual identity with 1931.
stages.reception: Affirmed as an approved official edition in circular 68/2009 until superseded by Blaj 2014 in May 2015.

stages.label: Blaj revised Liturghier (2014; promulgated official 20 May 2015)
stages.scope: Official Romanian Greek Catholic Liturghier incorporating linguistic corrections checked against the Greek, clarified typikon rubrics, Sunday/festal Vespers and Matins, and the 2006/2012 Pope and Major Archbishop commemoration formula.
stages.witness_label: Dumnezeieștile și Sfintele Liturghii ... precum și rânduiala Vecerniei și Utreniei din duminici și sărbători (Blaj, 2014)
stages.summary: Declared the official text by synodal circular of 20 May 2015 (effective on publication of the circular): retains the 1931 Blaj linguistic heritage while correcting wording against the Greek original (Băltăceanu & Broșteanu), clarifying typikon rubrics, appending Sunday/festal Vespers and Matins, and printing at pp. 80 and 104 the canonical Pope/Major Archbishop commemoration formula enacted by circular 723/2006 (amended 20 Feb 2012 to add 'cardinal').

evidence.claim: Promulgates Blaj 2014 as official text replacing Rome 1996 and specifies language corrections and clarified rubrics.
Firsthand editors document linguistic revision checked against the Greek text and theological usage.
Records full 2014 title and locates the 2006/2012 Pope and Major Archbishop commemoration formula at pp. 80 and 104.

stages.limitations: 2014 publication date and 20 May 2015 promulgation/effective date are kept distinct. Original 2014 book remains unacquired and uncollated by this project.
stages.reception: Promulgated as official across the Romanian Greek Catholic Major Archiepiscopal Church on 20 May 2015; uniform parish adoption not independently measured.

stages.label: Tiruvalla Syriac Xystus Taksa with Malayalam rubrics and reception appendix
stages.scope: Catholic-approved Syriac celebrant book for the Anaphora of Mar Xystus with Malayalam rubrics and printed absolution formulas for receiving converts and priests into Catholic communion.
stages.witness_label: Ṭeksā d-qurbānā (Anaphora of Mar Xystus), Tiruvalla: St. Joseph's Printing House, 1960
stages.summary: Directly inspected Catholic Syro-Malankara printing bearing Benedict Mar Gregorios's re-imprimatur of 11 May 1960 (implying an earlier unidentified approved edition); prints the Syriac Xystus liturgy with Malayalam rubrics and an appendix (printed p. 71) giving Syriac absolution formulas and Malayalam rubrics for receiving laity and clergy into Catholic communion.

evidence.claim: Title, Tiruvalla imprint, 11 May 1960 re-imprimatur, Syriac liturgical opening, and p. 71 reception-into-communion appendix directly inspected on page images.

stages.limitations: Full Syriac prayer body not transcribed or collated against 1934 Pampakuda; earlier edition implied by 're-imprimatur' remains unidentified.
stages.reception: Approved by Metropolitan Benedict Mar Gregorios for Syro-Malankara Catholic use; geographic extent of parish use unquantified.

stages.label: Tiruvalla Syriac Xystus Taksa (1965 imprimatur printing)
stages.scope: Subsequent Catholic-approved Tiruvalla printing of the Syriac–Malayalam Xystus Taksa (99 PDF pages); no substantive textual change from 1960 established.
stages.witness_label: Ṭeksā d-qurbānā (Anaphora of Mar Xystus, Patriarch of Rome), Tiruvalla: St. Joseph's Printing House, 1965
stages.summary: Directly inspected title and imprimatur of Benedict Mar Gregorios (2 February 1965) documenting a fresh Tiruvalla issue of the Syriac–Malayalam Mar Xystus Taksa immediately prior to the 1966 Malayalam-language edition.

evidence.claim: Original title leaf and 2 February 1965 imprimatur visually inspected.

stages.limitations: Body not collated against 1960; recorded as a printing/witness succession state rather than a substantive revision.
stages.reception: Episcopal imprimatur of Benedict Mar Gregorios; exact parish adoption unquantified.

stages.label: Hierarchically approved Malayalam Qurbana Taksa (St. Xystus)
stages.scope: Issued Malayalam-language St. Xystus Qurbana Taksa (160 PDF pages) prepared by the Liturgical Committee with joint episcopal preface; retained in origin/use review pending independent documentation of actual parish celebration.
stages.witness_label: സീറോ-മലങ്കര കുർബാന തക്സ / Syro-Malankara Qurbana Taksa (Puthusserry/Kallooppara: Kerala Printers, 1966)
stages.summary: Directly inspected scan of the Liturgical Committee's Malayalam St. Xystus Qurbana Taksa published by Rev. Thomas Pazhoor with stated hierarchical approval and a 1 January 1966 joint preface signed by Benedict Mar Gregorios (Trivandrum) and Zacharias Mar Athanasios (Tiruvalla).

evidence.locus: PDF p. 2 (title/imprint/approval) and PDF p. 7 / printed p. iv (joint episcopal preface)
evidence.claim: Directly verifies hierarchical approval statement, Liturgical Committee authorship, publisher/printer, and 1 January 1966 joint episcopal signatures.

stages.limitations: Per repository scope review (2026-10-20) under guidance/time-machine.md §11, publication and hierarchical preface do not yet supply independent proof of actual parish use; Malayalam body is uncollated against Tiruvalla 1960/1965 or 1934 Pampakuda.
stages.reception: Issued with joint episcopal preface of Trivandrum and Tiruvalla hierarchs; dated actual altar use remains pending verification.

stages.label: Nine-Anaphora Syro-Malankara Teksod-Qurobo
stages.scope: Expanded nine-anaphora Eucharistic repertoire attested in active Syro-Malankara use by Paniker (1991), expanding dramatically beyond the two-anaphora repertoire of Pampakuda 1934.
stages.witness_label: Order of the Holy Qurbono of the Syro-Malankara Church (Teksod-Qurobo), 1987 edition
stages.summary: Givergis Paniker Karichal (1991, p. 48) documents the 1987 Teksod-Qurobo then in active use, containing nine anaphoras: Minor James, John the Apostle, Twelve Apostles, Dionysius, Ivanios, Peter, Xystus, Eustathius, and the Doctors.

evidence.claim: Identifies the 1987 Teksod-Qurobo in active use and enumerates all nine anaphoras.

stages.limitations: Original 1987 printing remains unacquired and its exact language distribution (Malayalam vs Syriac) is not explicitly specified at Paniker p. 48. Distinct from the 1986 Syro-Malabar (East Syriac) Qurbana milestone.
stages.reception: Explicitly reported by Paniker (1991) as the Syro-Malankara edition then in active liturgical use.

stages.label: Synod-approved revised Malayalam Takso (approved 2006; released October 2007)
stages.scope: Synodal approval criteria and release of the revised nine-anaphora Malayalam Takso (Malankara Catholic Publications); distinct from the February 2007 Qurbonokramam and the separate October 2007 concelebration directions.
stages.witness_label: Revised Order of the Holy Qurbono (Takso), approved by Fourth Synod (2006), released Fifth Synod (October 2007)
stages.summary: Decision II.6 of the Fourth Ordinary Holy Episcopal Synod (31 Oct – 3 Nov 2006) approved the revised Malayalam Takso with named criteria: Malayalam translations of the nine anaphoras conformed to the Syriac, Syriac Institution Narrative and Epiclesis printed alongside Malayalam, St. Thomas added in the intercessions, kukilion revised, rubrics referred to the Thukasa except the three anaphora blessings, and Julius anaphora / long proemion-sedro / additional huthomo held in abeyance. Released by the Catholicos during the Fifth Synod (9–12 Oct 2007).

evidence.locus: Printed pp. 30–31 and Decision II.6 p. 46
evidence.claim: Primary synodal report and decision specifying the exact Malayalam/Syriac revisions, St. Thomas intercession addition, rubric deferral to Thukasa, and items held in abeyance.
Records official release of the revised Taksa during the Fifth Synod (9–12 October 2007), separate from the already published Qurbonakramam.
Confirms that the 2007 Malayalam Takso prints nine anaphoras (six translated in the 2023 eparchial English edition).

stages.limitations: Positioned at the 2006 approval event (distinct from October 2007 release). Original 2007 printed volume remains unacquired, and independent proof of actual parish celebration remains pending under guidance/time-machine.md §11.
stages.reception: Approved by the Holy Episcopal Synod (2006) and released by the Catholicos (October 2007); subsequent diaspora translations (English 2012/2023) draw on it, while parish-level implementation in Kerala remains unmeasured here.

stages.label: Vilnius Mamonych Sluzhebnik (first Catholic Ruthenian printing)
stages.scope: First Church Slavonic Sluzhebnik printed specifically for Catholic Ruthenians (Vilnius: Leon Mamonych, at Chancellor Lev Sapieha's expense), containing three liturgies, Presanctified, and a priest's Nauka mixing Eastern and Latin practice.
stages.witness_label: Книга Служебникъ (Vilnius: Leon Mamonych, 1617), 29+26 unnumbered leaves, pp. 1–473
stages.summary: Title and opening leaves directly inspected: issued without formal ecclesiastical approbation at Chancellor Lev Sapieha's expense; contains Chrysostom, Basil, Presanctified, Vespers, Matins, and a priest's Nauka blending Eastern and Latin rubrical usage, standing in direct contrast to the Orthodox Vilnius Holy Spirit Brotherhood Sluzhebnik of the same year (Kniga Belarusi no. 81, same pagination, no Nauka).

evidence.claim: Title leaf (1617, three liturgies and Presanctified, Mamonych press), Sapieha arms, dedication, and Nauka directly inspected.
Provides collation, 1 January 1617 dedication date, full contents list, and bibliographic contrast with the Orthodox Brotherhood edition.
Identifies Mamonych 1617 as the first Sluzhebnik produced for Catholic Ruthenians, without formal ecclesiastical approval, with a mixed Eastern–Latin Nauka.

stages.limitations: Title and opening leaves checked; full prayer body not collated leaf-by-leaf. Shared historical Kyivan Uniate metropolia witness, not exclusively modern Belarusian.
stages.reception: Printed for Catholic Ruthenians in the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth without formal hierarchical approbation; parish adoption extent unquantified.

stages.label: Supraśl post-Zamość Liturgikon (1727–1732 printing span)
stages.scope: Post-Synod of Zamość Church Slavonic Liturgikon prepared in the Żochowski tradition (RNB OR VII.3.15, 478 pp.), incorporating Filioque, St. Josaphat at Proskomedia, and papal/royal commemorations.
stages.witness_label: Леитоургикон си ест Служебник (Supraśl, begun 1727 under Lev Kyshka, completed 14 January 1732 under Atanasii Sheptytsky)
stages.summary: One continuous production span across two metropolitans prepared as the edition decreed by the Synod of Zamość (1720) in the Żochowski (1692–1695) line, though printed without Roman approbation; Senchenko's examination of RNB OR VII.3.15 documents St. Josaphat commemorated at Proskomedia, the Creed with Filioque, and commemorations of the Pope and King.

evidence.claim: Records 1727 title, 14 January 1732 colophon (p. 478), and RNB OR VII.3.15 liturgical features (Josaphat at Proskomedia, Filioque, papal and royal commemorations).
Identifies Supraśl 1727–1732 as the post-Zamość Żochowski-tradition edition printed without Roman approval.
Catalogues the first Supraśl impression ('первое типом издадеся') and its menaion/common-service components.

stages.limitations: RNB OR VII.3.15 original scan not acquired; structural discrepancy between Kniga Belarusi no. 209 contents summary and Senchenko's liturgy citations remains to be resolved on the physical copy.
stages.reception: Issued by the Supraśl Basilian monastery press for the Uniate metropolia (especially Belarusian–Lithuanian lands); later followed by the 1763 second impression.

stages.label: Supraśl Chrysostom Sluzhebnik for private/travelling priests with Western-patron propers
stages.scope: Portable Chrysostom-only Church Slavonic Sluzhebnik ([2]+174 pp.) explicitly for priests celebrating privately without singing and while travelling, appending named Latin-origin and Polish–Lithuanian patron propers.
stages.witness_label: Служебник в нем же литургиа ... Иоанна Златоустаго (Supraśl, 1758; RSL MK Кир. 2°)
stages.summary: Directly inspected NEB images verify the Cyrillic 1758 title's private/travelling purpose statement, Proskomedia, lay-communion admonition, and contents leaves listing propers for the Holy Eucharist, Most Sweet Name of Jesus, Passion, Conception/Visitation/Compassion/Rosary of the Mother of God, Bl. Josaphat, Francis, Dominic, Anthony of Padua, Ignatius Loyola, John Nepomucene, and Casimir (patrons of Poland and Lithuania).

evidence.claim: Title leaf (1758, private unsung/travelling celebration), Proskomedia opening, and full contents list of Western/patron propers visually inspected.
Corroborates collation ([2], 174 = 176 pp.) and Supraśl 1758 imprint.

stages.limitations: Single-liturgy portable component book rather than a full three-liturgy Liturgiarion; full text body not transcribed.
stages.reception: Printed at the Supraśl Basilian press for Uniate clergy across the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth.

stages.label: Pochaiv Liturgiarion (fourth impression, with 1754 Roman Greek rubrical affinities)
stages.scope: Fourth Pochaiv Church Slavonic Liturgiarion retaining the Żochowski framework while adopting selected rubrics similar to Benedict XIV's 1754 Roman Greek Euchologion.
stages.witness_label: Леітоургіаріон или Служебникъ ... Четвертое тупомъ издадеся (Pochaiv, 1788)
stages.summary: Directly inspected scan confirms the Cyrillic 1788 title (fourth impression, correcting the UGCC commission link's '1798' mislabel), 'Mirror for priests' preface, Proskomedia, and end contents; Huculak (1990) notes it follows the Żochowski tradition while incorporating rubrics resembling the 1754 Roman Greek Euchologion.

evidence.claim: Title (1788, fourth impression, Pochaiv), preface, Proskomedia, and contents visually inspected.
Records collation ([3]+114 ff.+14+[2]) and identifies Żochowski base with rubrics similar to Benedict XIV's 1754 Greek Euchologion.

stages.limitations: Shared Kyivan Uniate printing (Pochaiv, Volhynia) linked across Ukrainian and Belarusian Uniate heritage; body rubrics not independently collated against 1754.
stages.reception: Fourth impression at Pochaiv Basilian press; scanned copy bears later Lviv bookseller stamp and manuscript name lists.

stages.label: Modern Belarusian Liturgikon (Fr. Alexander Nadson, London; provisional lead)
stages.date_label: 2005 reported publication (preceded by 1999 priest's book and reported 2004 Minsk edition)
stages.scope: Modern Belarusian-language Greek Catholic Liturgikon translated by Fr. Alexander Nadson (London: Božym Šlacham, 2005); provisional bibliographic lead pending book inspection and approval verification.
stages.witness_label: Літургікон (London: Božym Šlacham, 2005; Fr. Alexander Nadson translation)
stages.summary: Community bibliography records Fr. Alexander Nadson's Belarusian Liturgikon (London 2005, edited by S. Stasievič and A. Trafimienka), capping decades of Belarusian translations from Greek and Church Slavonic alongside his 1999 Chrysostom priest's book, 2002 prayer book, and a reported 2004 Minsk Sluzhebnik.

evidence.claim: Identifies the 2005 London Літургікон and companion Belarusian Greek Catholic editions prepared by Fr. Alexander Nadson.

stages.limitations: Provisional stage backed only by an uninspected community bibliographic lead; original volume, formal ecclesiastical approbation, exact Greek/Slavonic exemplar, and relation to the reported 2004 Minsk printing remain unverified.
stages.reception: Reported in Belarusian Greek Catholic diaspora and post-Soviet community use; formal canonical approval and nationwide adoption remain to be verified.

stages.label: Slovenian Božja liturgija (Trieste and Rome, 1965)
stages.scope: Chrysostom and Basil Slovenian translation with rubrics and appended antiphons/dismissals (Latin Trieste imprimatur), serving as the documented before-state contrasted by the 2022–2023 official Slovenian Služebnik.
stages.witness_label: Božja liturgija sv. Janeza Zlatoustega in sv. Vasilija Velikega (Trieste and Rome, 1965; Markuža, Koren, Janežič)
stages.summary: Prepared by Jože Markuža, Anton Koren, and Stanko Janežič with nihil obstat of Jakob Ukmar and Latin imprimatur of Trieste vicar general Fortunato Fornasaro; Bogataj (2022) documents that its festal and daily antiphons were abridged and Sunday antiphons were omitted.

evidence.claim: Identifies the 1965 Trieste/Rome edition, its Latin imprimatur, and its abridged festal/daily antiphons and absent Sunday antiphons.

stages.limitations: Original 1965 booklet and its underlying Church Slavonic source edition were not independently inspected; carried a Latin-diocesan imprimatur rather than Eastern Congregation approval.
stages.reception: Used historically among Slovenian Greek Catholics within Križevci jurisdiction prior to the 2022–2023 official translation.

stages.label: Rome 1970 Grottaferrata Recensio ruthena Chrysostom printing (cited Križevci exemplar)
stages.scope: Church Slavonic Recensio ruthena Chrysostom printing issued at Grottaferrata in 1970 and explicitly named as the direct Izvornik of the 2018 Križevci Croatian Liturgikon.
stages.witness_label: Božestvennaja Liturgija ... Ioanna Zlatoustago (Rim: V tipografii kriptoferatskija obiteli, 1970, Recensio ruthena)
stages.summary: Explicitly identified on directly inspected p. 4 of the 2018 Križevci Croatian Chrysostom Liturgikon as its Church Slavonic source text. By analogy with Grottaferrata's documented photolithographic reissue practice (Kolupaev 2012), it is probably a later printing of the Roman 1940 Ruthenian Chrysostom rather than a new textual recension, pending inspection of its own colophon.

evidence.claim: Explicitly cites the Rome 1970 Grottaferrata Recensio ruthena Chrysostom printing as the direct source text.
Documents Grottaferrata monastery press photolithographic reissue practice for Roman Slavonic books.

stages.limitations: Original 1970 Grottaferrata copy and colophon remain unacquired; retained as a distinct printing witness without claiming a substantive textual change over Rome 1940.
stages.reception: Directly received as the Church Slavonic exemplar for the 2018 Croatian Križevci Chrysostom edition.

stages.label: Križevci Eparchy official Croatian Chrysostom Liturgikon (ad experimentum)
stages.date_label: Printed February 2018 (Congregation approval 2 Feb 2017; eparchial decree 30 Jan 2018)
stages.scope: Official Croatian translation of the Chrysostom Liturgy for the Križevci Eparchy, translated directly from Rome 1970 Recensio ruthena and authorized ad experimentum for five years.
stages.witness_label: Božanska liturgija svetog oca našega Ivana Zlatoustoga (Zagreb: Ordinarijat Križevačke eparhije, Feb 2018, ISBN 978-953-59968-0-4)
stages.summary: Directly image-inspected front matter (pp. 1, 3–5) verifies preparation by the eparchial liturgical council from the Rome 1970 Grottaferrata Recensio ruthena Chrysostom printing, Congregation for the Eastern Churches approval on 2 February 2017 (Prot. N. 64/2016), Bishop Nikola Kekić's decree no. 5/2018 (Zagreb, 30 January 2018) authorizing official liturgical use ad experimentum for five years, and a February 2018 print run of 1000 copies.

evidence.claim: Directly authenticates the 1970 source imprint, 2017 Holy See approval, 2018 eparchial decree, and February 2018 publication.

stages.limitations: Renewal or definitive confirmation after the five-year ad experimentum period (c. early 2023) remains unverified; applies to Croatian use in the Križevci Eparchy and does NOT evidence Serbian (Ruski Krstur) usage.
stages.reception: Authorized as official liturgical book of the Križevci Eparchy for five years ad experimentum by decree 5/2018.

stages.label: Official Slovenian Služebnik for the Križevci Eparchy (Chrysostom and Basil)
stages.scope: Official Slovenian celebrant Služebnik (with companion people's and notated volumes) translated directly from Rome 1942 Recensio ruthena, restoring antiphons and adding local Slovene first-millennium saints and St. Josaphat to the Proskomedia.
stages.witness_label: Služebnik. Božja liturgija Janeza Zlatoustega in Božja liturgija Bazilija Vélikega (Ljubljana: KUD Logos / Križevci Eparchy, 2022–2023)
stages.summary: Translated directly from the Rome 1942 Church Slavonic Ruthenian Liturgikon and approved by the Dicastery for the Eastern Churches (30 November 2022, Prot. 152/2022) and Bishop Milan Stipić (no. 14/2023); publicly presented in Ljubljana on 25 May 2023 in three role volumes (ISBN 978-961-7155-17-4). Restores the festal, daily, and Sunday antiphons abridged or omitted in 1965, and at the Dicastery's recommendation adds first-millennium saints of the Slovene lands (Maximilian of Celeia, Victorinus of Poetovio, Maximus of Emona, Jerome) and St. Josaphat Kuntsevych to the Proskomedia.

evidence.claim: Identifies the Rome 1942 source, Prot. 152/2022 approval, restored antiphons, added Proskomedia saints, and coexistence alongside Church Slavonic.
Confirms the 25 May 2023 presentation of three role volumes, 30 Nov 2022 Dicastery approval, Bishop Stipić decree 14/2023, and KUD Logos/Križevci co-publication.

stages.limitations: Original signed decrees (Prot. 152/2022, no. 14/2023) and complete printed volumes remain unacquired; which of the three volumes bears ISBN 978-961-7155-17-4 is unstated.
stages.reception: Official Slovenian liturgical edition for Križevci Eparchy faithful in Slovenia; Bogataj notes it stands alongside, rather than replacing, Church Slavonic.

stages.label: First printed Hungarian Chrysostom (1882) and complementary Basil/Presanctified (1890) volumes
stages.scope: Two complementary Debrecen-printed Hungarian service volumes prepared by the 1879 Mukachevo/Prešov consistories committee (without ecclesiastical approval), forming the direct base combined and revised in 1920.
stages.witness_label: Debrecen 1882 Chrysostom (90+2 pp.) and Debrecen 1890 Basil/Presanctified/offices (103+2 pp.)
stages.summary: The nine-member committee formed at Hajdúdorog in 1879 compiled the 1882 Chrysostom volume (Debrecen, 90+2 pp., without ecclesiastical approval) from multiple Church Slavonic versions including Mohylan/Pochaiv/Lviv special-intention formularies and paschal rites; Emil Melles and János Danilovics supplied the complementary 1890 volume (Debrecen: Kutasi Imre, 103+2 pp.) containing Basil, Presanctified, priestly office prayers, and the Great Canon.

evidence.claim: Describes the 1882 committee compilation from multiple Slavonic versions, absence of ecclesiastical approval, Mohylan/Lviv intention formularies, and the 1890 complement.
Records exact titles and extents of 1882 and 1890 and identifies them as the two separate volumes combined and revised in 1920.

stages.limitations: Full 1882 and 1890 volumes remain unacquired; carried no formal ecclesiastical approbation, so public-use authorization is not inferred.
stages.reception: Foundational printed Hungarian liturgical corpus preceding the erection of the Hajdúdorog Eparchy (1912) and the 1920/1921 revised Liturgikon.

stages.label: Hajdúdorog Gregorian calendar reform (circulars 1990/1916 and 3150/1916)
stages.scope: Episcopal calendar enactment moving Hajdúdorog feasts to the Gregorian calendar from 24 June 1916, with supplementary rules for three named autumn feasts.
stages.witness_label: Bishop István Miklósy circulars 1990/1916 (Körlevelek VI, p. 25) and 3150/1916 (Körlevelek XI, p. 52)
stages.summary: Following a 4 May 1916 conference with the Mukachevo and Prešov bishops, Bishop Miklósy enacted the Gregorian calendar from 24 June 1916 (circular 1990/1916), supplemented by circular 3150/1916 making separate provision for the Exaltation of the Cross, St. Demetrius, and the Protection of the Theotokos. Mukachevo restored the Julian calendar in November 1918 and some Hajdúdorog parishes temporarily reverted in 1919.

evidence.claim: Documents the 4 May decision, 24 June 1916 effective date, circular 1990/1916, supplementary circular 3150/1916, and uneven 1918–1919 regional observance.

stages.limitations: Original printed circulars in GMFL I–1–h not acquired; uneven 1919 compliance demonstrates that effective date does not prove uninterrupted universal observance.
stages.reception: Enacted for the Hajdúdorog Eparchy; calendar and 1921–1960 paschalion subsequently printed in the 1920 Liturgikon.

stages.label: Miklósy circulars omitting ruler petitions (1918) and revising Holy Cross propers (1919)
stages.scope: Targeted post-abdication prayer and proper-text directives in the Hajdúdorog Eparchy immediately preceding the 1920/1921 Liturgikon.
stages.witness_label: Miklósy circulars 4471/1918 and 808/1919 (quoted via Ivancsó 2007)
stages.summary: Following the 1918 imperial abdication, circular 4471/1918 removed prayers and litany petitions for the sovereign, and circular 808/1919 substituted the country for the ruler in the Holy Cross troparion and kontakion.

evidence.claim: Documents circulars 4471/1918 (omission of ruler petitions) and 808/1919 (Holy Cross troparion/kontakion substitution).

stages.limitations: Circular originals remain unacquired; component-level directives rather than a full altar book.
stages.reception: Eparchial normative directives for Hajdúdorog parishes.

stages.label: Bishop Miklós Dudás's Solemn Chrysostom Rubrical Instruction
stages.scope: Episcopal rubrical codification for solemn celebration of the Chrysostom Liturgy (Nyíregyháza, 1954), standardizing existing practice to prevent abridgements and anomalies rather than enacting a liturgical reform.
stages.witness_label: Szertartási utasítások Aranyszájú Szent János Liturgiájának ünnepélyes bemutatásához (Nyíregyháza, 1954; circular 819/1954)
stages.summary: Issued by Bishop Miklós Dudás both as a Nyíregyháza instruction booklet and as ordinance 819 in circular 1954/XIII on uniform celebration of the liturgy and sacraments; Dobos (2020) characterizes it as a codification of existing ceremonial order designed to curb arbitrary abbreviations.

evidence.claim: Records Dudás's 1954 Nyíregyháza instruction and ordinance 819/1954 as a codification of existing solemn celebration rubrics.
Confirms the 1954 Dudás rubrical ordinance and its anti-abridgement purpose.

stages.limitations: Printed 1954 directive and circular 1954/XIII original remain unacquired; no textual change to prayers or anaphoras asserted.
stages.reception: Issued for the Hajdúdorog Eparchy; a manuscript copy is separately reported in Kántorjánosi parish records.

stages.label: Bulgarian Sluzhebnik of Georgi Eldarov (contents-verified witness)
stages.scope: Complete Bulgarian Cyrillic celebrant service book attested directly by photographed contents leaves (pp. 615–617), covering preparatory rites, three Byzantine liturgies, Latin-associated heart propers, a full twelve-month calendar, and postcommunion prayers.
stages.witness_label: Служебник (Георги Елдъров, Rome 1985; photographed contents leaves pp. 615–617)
stages.summary: Three directly inspected photographs of printed contents leaves pp. 615–617 establish a comprehensive Bulgarian Cyrillic celebrant book: preparatory rites (pp. 7–12), Chrysostom (p. 20), Basil (p. 63), Presanctified (p. 105), Sacred Heart (p. 301) and Immaculate Heart (p. 306) propers, January–December calendar (pp. 319–571), and postcommunion prayers (p. 609). Seller metadata attributes 617 pages, the Vatican Polyglot Press, and permission of Exarch Methodius, which remain to be verified on the title and approval leaves.

evidence.locus: Directly viewed photographs of printed contents leaves pp. 615–617
evidence.claim: Verifies full Bulgarian Cyrillic celebrant contents including all three Byzantine liturgies, Sacred/Immaculate Heart propers, and full liturgical calendar.

stages.limitations: Title leaf, approval leaf, and source-edition statement were not photographed; does NOT prove reception of the 1942 Roman Slavonic Vulgata or distinguish original adaptation from translation.
stages.reception: Seller attributes Exarch Methodius's permission; original approbation and parish adoption in Bulgaria remain to be independently verified.

stages.label: Holy See recognitio / approval of Macedonian Chrysostom and Basil Liturgies
stages.scope: Official Holy See approval/recognitio act for the Macedonian translation of the Divine Liturgies of St. John Chrysostom and St. Basil the Great; distinct from the unauthenticated printed Литургикон (2009) title lead.
stages.witness_label: Congregation for the Eastern Churches act of 9 December 2009 (SICO 2009 p. 291; official register line 41)
stages.summary: Two directly inspected official Holy See sources document the 9 December 2009 ecclesiastical action authorizing Macedonian translations of the Divine Liturgies of St. John Chrysostom and St. Basil the Great for the Macedonian Greek Catholic Church (then Apostolic Exarchate in Macedonia, elevated in 2018 to the Eparchy of Strumica–Skopje). SICO 2009 records the act under 'recognitio', while the Congregation's web register labels it 'approval'; both terms are preserved.

evidence.locus: SICO Anno 2009, LXIV, printed p. 291 / PDF p. 290, final recognitio bullet
evidence.claim: Records official Holy See recognitio dated 9 December 2009 for Macedonian Chrysostom and Basil Liturgies.
Corroborates the 9 December 2009 dated action for Macedonian Chrysostom and Basil under the register's approval heading.

stages.limitations: Documents the normative Holy See approval act only; does NOT authenticate the unverified third-party Scribd extract listing Литургикон (2009) and companion books, does NOT identify the underlying Greek or Church Slavonic exemplar (pre-2001 Križevci jurisdiction alone cannot prove Rome 1942 Ruthenian dependence), and does NOT establish dated operative parish celebration (Bishop Stojanov's 2023 pastoral letter requests thanksgiving liturgies without naming a book or language).
stages.reception: Official Holy See authorization for the Macedonian Greek Catholic Church; printed altar edition and dated operative reception remain open gaps.

transitions.summary: Athanasios Dabbas's 1701 Snagov Greek–Arabic Liturgikon receives Meletios Karmé's 1612 Arabic recension beside an independent Venice Greek text.

evidence.claim: Identifies Karmé's 1612 Arabic revision as the Arabic text printed in Snagov 1701 alongside a non-parallel Venice Greek column.

transitions.limitations: Scholarly textual identification by Charon; no project-level collation between Karmé manuscripts and Snagov 1701.

transitions.summary: Propaganda Fide's 1839 Rome Liturgikon revises the shared Snagov 1701 text by adding papal commemoration, suppressing the diptychs, and conforming communion prayers to the Roman Greek Euchologion.

changes.before: Pre-1724 Snagov 1701 text lacked Catholic papal commemoration and retained the older diptychs and Antiochian communion-prayer wording.
changes.after: Rome 1839 introduces papal commemoration, suppresses the diptychs, and conforms the communion prayers to the Roman Greek Euchologion text.
changes.locus_before: Snagov 1701 and annotated Greek College correction copy as described in Charon 1908, pp. 545–565
changes.locus_after: Rome 1839 Propaganda Liturgikon (280 pp.) as described in Charon 1908, pp. 565–575, table p. 591

evidence.claim: Enumerates papal commemoration addition, diptych removal, and communion-prayer conformity to Roman Greek in 1839.

changes.before: Snagov 1701 intercession/commemoration structure reflected pre-1724 shared Antiochian usage.
changes.after: Rome 1839 adapts intercessory commemoration within the anaphoral framework to explicitly commemorate the Roman Pontiff while omitting the older diptychs.
changes.locus_before: Snagov 1701 as described in Charon 1908, pp. 555–565
changes.locus_after: Rome 1839 as described in Charon 1908, pp. 565–575

evidence.claim: Reports the 1839 commemoration and diptych modifications relative to 1701.
Directly contrasts Snagov 1701 (and the 1743 correction project) with the printed 1839 Propaganda edition.

transitions.limitations: Scholarly description by Charon; original 1701 and 1839 Arabic–Greek volumes were not directly collated by this project.

transitions.summary: The 1862 Vienna Liturgikon deliberately reproduces Propaganda 1839 in identical typographic disposition for free Melkite distribution, without establishing a new textual recension.

evidence.claim: States that Vienna 1862 reprints 1839 in the same disposition and retains the Roman Euchologion text.

transitions.limitations: Reprint succession described by Charon; not an independent leaf-by-leaf collation.

transitions.summary: Rahmé's 1899–1900 Beirut Liturgikon restyles the 1839 Arabic rubrics, prints the diaconal litany in full, and inserts a new Pope–Patriarch–Bishop commemoration formula explicitly contrasted with Propaganda 1839.

changes.before: Propaganda 1839 carried older Arabic rubric phrasing and abbreviated diaconal litany layout.
changes.after: Rahmé 1900 restyles the Arabic rubrics (without altering sense), prints the diaconal litany in full, and appends a new preface and appendix.
changes.locus_before: Rome 1839 as described in Charon 1908, pp. 565–575
changes.locus_after: Beirut 1900 (343 pp.) as described in Charon 1908, pp. 584–591

evidence.claim: Describes restyled rubrics, full diaconal litany, and added editorial apparatus in Rahmé 1900.

changes.before: Propaganda 1839 lacked the combined Pope–Patriarch–Bishop commemoration formula printed by Rahmé.
changes.after: Rahmé 1900 adds at pp. 140–141 a commemoration formula for Pope, patriarch, and bishop with an explicit editorial note stating it is not in the Propaganda book.
changes.locus_before: Absence in Propaganda 1839 expressly noted in Rahmé 1900 pp. 140–141 (via Charon 1908)
changes.locus_after: Beirut 1900 pp. 140–141 as reported in Charon 1908, pp. 584–591

evidence.claim: Quotes Rahmé's explicit contrast between his pp. 140–141 commemoration formula and the Propaganda 1839 book.
Compares Rahmé 1899/1900 directly against the 1839 Propaganda Liturgikon.

transitions.limitations: Scholarly comparison by Charon; Charon observes he never heard the pp. 140–141 formula used aloud. Original 1839 and 1900 copies uncollated here.

transitions.summary: Mo'aqqad's 1883 patriarchally approved Horologion revises the Choueir Horologion line (1787–1879) by correcting Arabic, restoring Psalms 33 and 144 to the Typika, and adding proper Melkite Catholic troparia.

changes.before: Choueir Horologion printings (1787, 1852, 1879) circulated unchanged without formal patriarchal revision, omitting Psalms 33 and 144 from the Typika and lacking the later Melkite Catholic proper troparia.
changes.after: Mo'aqqad's 1883 Horologion (736 pp., approved by Patriarch Gregory II Youssef) corrects the Arabic, restores Psalms 33 and 144 to the Typika, adds an appendix, and inserts troparia for offices proper to Melkite Catholics.
changes.locus_before: Choueir Horologion (1787, 1852, 1879), Charon 1908, p. 599
changes.locus_after: Mo'aqqad Horologion (1883), Charon 1908, pp. 599–602

evidence.claim: Contrasts the identical Choueir Horologion printings (1852 examined in hand) with Mo'aqqad's 1883 revised edition.
